# Peptides Weekly
> **A coroner links a 75-year-old's cardiac arrest to CJC-1295 and ipamorelin.**

**What You Need to Know:** A Victorian coroner has linked actor Richard Norton's cardiac arrest to two prescribed but unapproved peptides, CJC-1295 and ipamorelin, and asked Australia's regulator to reconsider whether doctors should be able to prescribe them. In the United States, a new enforcement-discretion policy temporarily opens compounding of six other unapproved peptides that FDA scientists had opposed. Separate company reports describe investigational GLP-1 results in people with diabetes, while published work on compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide shows quality gaps that marketing claims do not close.

### The Week in Peptides
**Coroner calls for TGA to review unapproved peptides after death of Australian actor: The Guardian**
Richard Norton, 75, an Australian actor, stuntman and fight choreographer, went into cardiac arrest in March 2025 after injecting prescribed but unapproved CJC-1295 and ipamorelin. This is a coronial finding, not a clinical trial: Victorian coroner David Ryan found the arrest followed those injections and was not satisfied the peptides should remain available for doctors to prescribe. Norton had asked medical practitioner Jerzy Muchnicki about peptide therapy in March 2025; the coroner's report says they discussed the experimental nature of the treatment, potential risks, and the lack of Therapeutic Goods Administration-approved alternatives. He had earlier been prescribed peptides by another practitioner for fatigue, shoulder pain and loss of muscle mass. Blood tests were used to check baseline health and contraindications, and Norton signed a consent form that included anaphylaxis among the risks. He was prescribed the two injections on 19 March. Ryan recommended the TGA review benefits and safety and consider moving the peptides from Schedule 4, prescription-only, to Schedule 10, limited to clinical trials or other experimental use, because therapeutic benefit is uncertain and safety risks are not fully known. ABC News reports the death may be the first confirmed fatality linked to unapproved peptides. Source: [theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/oct/29/peptide-actor-richard-norton-death-coroner-tga-review-ntwnfb)
Source: [abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-29/victoria-peptide-death-coroners-report-richard-norton/107320590)

**US Health Secretary RFK Jr to expand access to unapproved peptides: BBC**
A week after compounding rules were still an open regulatory question, Health and Human Services published an enforcement-discretion policy rather than another advisory vote. In a regulatory action, not a finding that the drugs work, Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. released plans, announced in the Federal Register, to let compounding pharmacies prepare six peptides the FDA has not approved: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, Semax and Epitalon. The draft came from the health secretary's office rather than the FDA. After official publication, a two-week public comment period follows. An FDA advisory panel voted in July to loosen restrictions; FDA staff recommended against that step. HHS says it will not pursue state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed doctors who compound those six if they follow rules on ingredient quality, manufacturing, safety reporting, labeling and prescriptions written for individual patients. The policy is temporary while the FDA finishes formal rulemaking on the bulk-substance list. Compounders must report serious adverse events and quality problems such as contamination. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Kennedy has called himself a big fan of the drugs and has described using BPC-157 for a muscle injury; that personal report is not evidence of benefit. The Partnership for Safe Medicines said the decision leaves a grey area, that FDA scientists had recommended against the substances over evidence concerns, and that many newly appointed Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee members appear to have conflicts of interest. PSM filed a citizen petition last week urging the FDA to disregard the vote, citing insufficient evidence and arguing the committee was constituted in violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act and the Ethics in Government Act. BBC reporting also notes unregulated injectable peptides marketed online for unproven uses, including to teenagers, with experts citing a lack of human trials and unknown long-term effects. Source: [bbc.com](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmq8nwd748v3o)
Source: [newsable.asianetnews.com](https://newsable.asianetnews.com/markets/hims-stock-jumps-5-after-hhs-temporarily-clears-compounding-of-six-peptides-articleshow-5g4gv33)
Source: [safemedicines.org](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/10/statement-on-503a-peptide-enforcement.html)
Source: [news.ssbcrack.com](https://news.ssbcrack.com/hhs-plan-for-peptide-drug-access-faces-fda-opposition-amid-safety-concerns/)

**Lilly's retatrutide bests Novo's Ozempic in head-to-head diabetes study: STAT News**
Eli Lilly said its investigational drug retatrutide was more effective at lowering blood sugar and cutting weight than Novo Nordisk's Ozempic in a large diabetes study. That claim is a company report of a head-to-head study in people with diabetes, not a published peer-reviewed paper in this week's sources. Retatrutide is investigational. Ozempic is the FDA-approved semaglutide brand for type 2 diabetes. Source: [statnews.com](https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/28/biotech-news-lillys-triple-g-drug-beats-ozempic-in-head-to-head-study/?utm_campaign=rss)
Source: [firstwordpharma.com](https://firstwordpharma.com/story/8314293)

**Ascletis' Oral Small Molecule GLP-1, ASC30, Demonstrated Placebo-Adjusted HbA1c Reduction of 1.7% at 12 Weeks from Its U.S. Phase II Study in Participants with Diabetes: PR Newswire**
Ascletis reported that ASC30, an investigational oral small-molecule GLP-1 rather than a peptide, produced a placebo-adjusted HbA1c reduction of 1.7 percent at 12 weeks in a U.S. phase II study in participants with diabetes. Source: [prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/ascletis-oral-small-molecule-glp-1--asc30--demonstrated-placebo-adjusted-hba1c-reduction-of-1-7-at-12-weeks-from-its-us-phase-ii-study-in-participants-with-diabetes-302922287.html)

**Hair Loss Associated With GLP-1 RAs Appear Similar by Race: Medscape**
Medscape reports that hair loss associated with GLP-1 receptor agonists appeared similar by race. That is an observational association as framed by the headline, not a randomized trial result and not evidence that the drugs cause hair loss equally, or at all, in every group. Source: [medscape.com](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/hair-loss-associated-glp-1-ras-appear-similar-race-2026a10014r5)

### Also Today
**Tirzepatide linked to lower short-term endometrial cancer risk in large cohort study: Bioengineer.org**
A large cohort study, an observational association and not a randomized trial, linked tirzepatide to a lower short-term risk of endometrial cancer. Source: [bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/tirzepatide-linked-to-lower-short-term-endometrial-cancer-risk-in-large-cohort-study/)

**Semaglutide shows early bone-building signal in male mice study: Bioengineer.org**
In male mice, an animal study and not a human result, semaglutide showed an early bone-building signal. Source: [bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/semaglutide-shows-early-bone-building-signal-in-male-mice-study/)

**Peptide-related death spurs call for telehealth inquiry: Medical Republic**
Medical Republic reports that the peptide-related death has spurred a call for a telehealth inquiry. Source: [medicalrepublic.com.au](https://www.medicalrepublic.com.au/peptide-related-death-spurs-call-for-telehealth-inquiry/130477)

### Peptide Spotlight: Compounding, Shortages and Copies
A 2025 search of compounding websites found 33 semaglutide or tirzepatide products whose strength, route or added ingredients differed from FDA-approved versions. That survey, published in the Annals of Pharmacotherapy, is the clearest recent map of what "a compounded GLP-1" has meant on the U.S. market.

Pharmacy compounding means a pharmacy prepares a medicine for a patient rather than dispensing the manufacturer's approved product. For semaglutide and tirzepatide, shortage rules had been the practical opening for copies. Semaglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist: a peptide that acts at the GLP-1 receptor and, in its approved forms, is used to lower blood sugar and, at the Wegovy brand, to treat overweight or obesity. A narrative review in the American Journal of Managed Care states that semaglutide is FDA-approved as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for overweight or obesity. High demand, social-media attention, shortages and cost then drew both legal and illegal compounded versions. The Annals paper's premise is the next regulatory step: once the shortage of the innovator products was resolved, compounding pharmacies could legally sell only unique products — a different route, a different dosing approach, or extra pharmaceutical ingredients — not simple copies of the approved drugs.

The same Annals survey, a product survey and not a trial, searched compounding sites from February 3 to March 20, 2025. Two-thirds of the 33 products contained semaglutide and one-third contained tirzepatide. Forty-eight percent combined semaglutide or tirzepatide with some mix of cyanocobalamin, glycine, niacinamide, docusate or ondansetron. Of 17 single-ingredient products, 82 percent were sublingual and 18 percent were oral disintegrating tablets. Only 18 percent reported a beyond-use date, and 28 percent reported preferred storage conditions. The authors found little justification for adding nutrients or docusate sodium to combination subcutaneous products. They saw a rationale for adding ondansetron, but not evidence that giving it under the skin works for this purpose. They also saw a rationale for sublingual or disintegrating-tablet forms, but not a determination that those forms beat innovator oral tablets. Their conclusion is that safety and efficacy of these compounded products are largely unknown.

A separate laboratory analysis, not a human study, tested compounded tirzepatide combined with vitamin B12 analogs from U.S. sources. Expert Opinion on Drug Safety reports a widespread, previously unidentified impurity formed by a chemical reaction between tirzepatide and certain B12 analogs, present at substantial levels. Those combinations had been mass-marketed as comparable to FDA-approved tirzepatide even though they undergo no evaluation of potency or impurity profiles, and they continued to be sold as "personalized" treatments. Clinical effects of the impurity are unknown. The finding is analytical chemistry: it shows a quality defect, not what that defect does in a person.

The human evidence in these papers is thinner than the marketing. A retrospective study in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism followed 94 people, 81 women and 13 men, mean age 46.57 years, in a commercial wellness-studio weight program who received once-weekly compounded semaglutide with cyanocobalamin between June 2023 and January 2024. After three months, average weight loss was 4.11 kilograms, or 4.57 percent. Fat mass fell by 2.67 kilograms and trunk fat by 1.10 kilograms. Lean mass fell by 1.43 kilograms and skeletal muscle mass by 0.88 kilograms. As a share of total weight, fat mass decreased while the proportions of lean mass and skeletal muscle increased. This is observational and uncontrolled. It is not a randomized comparison with FDA-approved semaglutide, and it cannot show that the compounded product matches the approved drug.

Harms show up in a case series, not a trial. The Journal of the American Pharmacists Association described three adverse-event reports to a regional poison control center after incorrect administration of semaglutide obtained for weight loss from compounding pharmacies and an aesthetic spa. Two patients self-administered tenfold dosing errors. All three had nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, with most symptoms lasting days. One also had headache, anorexia, weakness and fatigue. One sought care and responded to an antiemetic and intravenous fluids. One received a vial and syringes with no pharmacist counseling. One reported dosing in milliliters and units rather than milligrams. The authors note that vials lack the safety features of prefilled manufactured pens and can allow large overdoses. The American Journal of Managed Care review, a narrative review rather than new patient data, adds that compounded semaglutide on the market may lack historical quality controls and that fraudulent batches have appeared worldwide.

What is not established is as important as what was measured. No paper here shows that a compounded copy has the potency, impurity profile or clinical effect of Ozempic, Wegovy or approved tirzepatide. The impurity's clinical effects are unknown. Advantages of sublingual or disintegrating compounded tablets over approved oral tablets are not determined. The 94-person weight change is not proof the compound is safe or equivalent. Three poison-center cases cannot estimate how often errors occur.

Regulatory status, as these sources state it: Ozempic and Wegovy are FDA-approved semaglutide products for the uses named above. Compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide products are not FDA-approved. After the innovator shortage resolved, the Annals paper states that pharmacies could legally sell only unique products. Unapproved combinations carry purity, contamination, dosing-error and fraud risks that the approved pen products were built to limit.

What it is: Pharmacy compounding here means a pharmacy-made semaglutide or tirzepatide product that is not the FDA-approved manufacturer's drug.
Humans given it: A retrospective study followed 94 people on compounded semaglutide with cyanocobalamin, and a poison-center series describes three error cases; these sources include no randomized trial of the compounded products.
Regulatory status: Semaglutide is FDA-approved as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for overweight or obesity, while the compounded products in these papers are not FDA-approved.
Risks: Testing found a widespread tirzepatide-B12 impurity of unknown clinical effect, and case reports describe tenfold dosing errors, multi-day gastrointestinal symptoms, missing counseling and fraudulent batches.
What it does not show: None of this shows that compounded copies match approved products in potency, purity, safety or weight-loss effect.

### Worth Knowing
- A coroner's finding, not a trial, treated prescribed CJC-1295 and ipamorelin as unapproved drugs whose benefit is uncertain and whose risks are not fully known.
- Company reports of retatrutide and of oral ASC30 are early human signals in diabetes, not proof a listener can treat as settled comparative evidence.
- In people given compounded semaglutide outside a trial, weight fell and so did some lean and muscle mass; that observational pattern is not the same as a randomized result for an approved pen.
- A three-patient case series shows that vial-and-syringe compounded semaglutide can be measured wrong, with days of nausea, vomiting and pain — a harm signal, not a rate.

### Evidence Ledger
- A website survey identified 33 unique compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide products, many with added ingredients or non-injection forms, and found safety and efficacy largely unknown; product survey, not a trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41689811
- Laboratory testing found a widespread impurity in compounded tirzepatide combined with certain B12 analogs; analytical study, clinical effects unknown. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42010938
- Semaglutide is FDA-approved as Ozempic and Wegovy, and compounded versions have raised safety, efficacy and fraud concerns; narrative review. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40966636
- Ninety-four people on compounded semaglutide with cyanocobalamin lost weight and some lean mass over three months; retrospective observational study. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/39776038
- Three poison-center cases followed incorrect administration of compounded semaglutide, including two tenfold errors; case series. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37392810

Unapproved does not mean "almost approved" — it means the human evidence and the quality checks are not there yet.

# Peptides Weekly
> **Thirty-nine percent of GLP-1 users reported nail detachment, versus nine percent of controls.**

**What You Need to Know:** In a cross-sectional comparison presented at a dermatology congress, thirty-nine percent of GLP-1 users reported nail detachment, versus nine percent of people who had never taken the drugs. A separate surgical-record analysis linked the same drug class to slightly lower odds of combined heart and infection problems after planned operations. Neither finding is a randomized trial, and neither is a reason to start or stop a medicine.

### The Week in Peptides
**GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Nail and Hair Problems: Labroots**
At the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology Congress 2026, Charles Taïeb’s team presented a cross-sectional comparison, not a randomized trial, of 575 people using GLP-1 receptor agonists and 1,329 people with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes who had never taken them, recruited in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico. Nail detachment was reported by 39 percent of users and 9 percent of controls, nail discoloration by 46 percent versus 17 percent, and at least one nail disorder by 66 percent versus 53 percent. Detachment and discoloration stayed about two to three times as common after the comparison was limited to people who had lost weight and after skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies were accounted for. In the same participants, unusual hair loss was 50 percent versus 34 percent, reduced hair volume or density 42 percent versus 19 percent, hair loss beginning after treatment started 26 percent versus 12 percent, and scalp redness about three times as common, often with itching, redness, or scaling. Taïeb said the association is clear, and that not everything during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment. Both studies used participant-reported symptoms, and about half of medication users also reported nail problems before starting treatment. Source: [labroots.com](https://www.labroots.com/trending/digestive-system/31257/glp-1-drugs-linked-nail-hair/amp)

**GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Fewer Heart Complications and Infections After Surgery, New Study Finds: Yahoo**
An observational analysis presented on October 18 at the ANESTHESIOLOGY 2026 meeting in San Diego, led by Josephine Tolan of McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and drawn from the Epic Cosmos record system, is not a randomized trial. It covered U.S. adults in elective surgery from January 2016 through December 2024, limited to operations longer than 60 minutes with at least 24 hours in hospital: 2,028,601 patients, including 145,610 taking GLP-1 medications, about 7 percent. After matching, users had 11 percent lower odds of major cardiovascular complications and 8 percent lower odds of postoperative infections. Those cardiovascular events were a combined set of heart attacks, heart injury, strokes, and deaths, and the infections were a combined set of surgical-site infection, urinary tract infection, pneumonia, and sepsis, so the percentages do not apply to any one of those events; emergency operations, shorter procedures, and same-day discharges were excluded. In a tighter match of 114,249 users and 360,168 nonusers, with adjustment for diabetes and earlier opioid and NSAID use, major cardiovascular complications occurred in 1.0 percent of users and 1.1 percent of nonusers, and postoperative infections in 4.9 percent and 5.3 percent. Source: [yahoo.com](https://www.yahoo.com/news/science/articles/glp-1-drugs-linked-fewer-144330546.html)

**Partnership for Safe Medicines Files Citizen Petition Urging FDA to Block Compounding of Unapproved and Uncharacterized Peptides: Partnership for Safe Medicines**
On October 16 the Partnership for Safe Medicines filed a citizen petition, a regulatory request rather than a clinical study, asking the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to block compounding by any route of seven unapproved peptides — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, emideltide, semax, and epitalon — and to disregard a July Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee vote as a basis for future rulemaking. Agency scientists had recommended against bulk compounding of all seven; the committee voted to allow six of the seven, and the petition argues that newly appointed members had financial ties to the peptide industry and that the meeting violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act and the Ethics in Government Act. Executive director Shabbir Imber Safdar said FDA scientists found no adequate characterization, extremely limited safety data, and no meaningful human evidence, and briefing documents stated that none of the substances had been adequately tested in human trials. The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding said in September 2026 that 503A pharmacies may not legally compound them now, yet licensed pharmacies are still selling them. To show the enforcement gap, PSM bought several of the peptides, and four pharmacies in Texas and Pennsylvania compounded, dispensed, and shipped them to California within 45 days. The same filing notes that FDA has received reports of two patients who died after taking illegally compounded retatrutide, an unapproved product outside this list of seven. Source: [safemedicines.org](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/10/press-release-psm-petition-peptides.html)
Source: [safemedicines.org](https://www.safemedicines.org/2026/10/psm-files-citizen-petitio.html)

**A bipartisan group of lawmakers urges the FDA to close a peptide loophole: STAT**
A bipartisan group of lawmakers is urging the FDA to close a loophole used to import knockoff retatrutide, STAT reported, which is a legislative request rather than new trial evidence. Retatrutide is an investigational obesity drug made by Eli Lilly, so a knockoff import is not an approved medicine. Source: [statnews.com](https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/20/health-policy-news-bipartisan-group-of-lawmaker-urges-fda-to-close-peptide-loophole/)
Source: [statnews.com](https://www.statnews.com/2026/10/20/health-policy-news-bipartisan-group-of-lawmaker-urges-fda-to-close-peptide-loophole/?utm_campaign=rss)

**Semaglutide and teduglutide reduce immune-driven gut injury in mice: News-Medical**
A mouse study reported by News-Medical found that semaglutide and teduglutide reduced immune-driven gut injury, which is an animal result and not a human result. Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist; this report does not move that animal finding into a new human indication. Source: [news-medical.net](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20261021/Semaglutide-and-teduglutide-reduce-immune-driven-gut-injury-in-mice.aspx)

### Also Today
**TikTok Blocks Peptide Searches: What Women Should Know: EEW Magazine**
TikTok is blocking peptide searches, a platform restriction on how those products are found rather than a new study of their effects. Source: [eewmagazineonline.com](https://www.eewmagazineonline.com/health-and-wellness/2026/10/20/tiktok-blocks-peptide-searches)

**Peptide surge hits NSW hospitals: New England Times**
Hospitals in New South Wales are seeing a surge in peptide-related presentations, a clinical-service signal rather than a trial result. Source: [netimes.com.au](https://www.netimes.com.au/2026/10/20/peptide-surge-hits-nsw-hospitals/)

### Peptide Spotlight: The Research Use Only Market
A legal loophole lets consumers buy peptide semaglutide without a prescription, and the websites that sell it do not sell the supplies or provide guidance. That is the opening fact in a Public Health Reports study of what happens next, when an untrained adult tries to turn that purchase into an injection using only what they can find online. The research-use label, and the grey-market vial that travels with it, is a sales description. It is not a finding that a regulator has reviewed the product for identity, dose accuracy, sterility, or a human benefit.

The study asked a narrow question about how this market is actually used. From September 1, 2025, through January 30, 2026, investigators recruited college students at the University of Connecticut and older adults, twenty people in all, twelve men and eight women, with a mean age of forty years and a standard deviation of twenty-one. Participants looked up information online. The team then handed them various semaglutide and diluent vials and supplies and scored thirty-four steps, one point for each step completed successfully. Confidence was rated from one, no confidence, to five, complete confidence. This was not a treatment trial. Nobody’s weight, blood sugar, or symptoms were the outcome. The outcome was whether an adult without training could carry out the preparation.

They completed fifteen of the thirty-four steps correctly. The mean score was forty-four percent, with a standard deviation of fifty percent, so the group was not tightly clustered around that average. Errors were the kind that could result in incorrect dosing, needle sticks, or infections. Mean confidence was two point three before the demonstration and one point nine after it, and that drop was not statistically significant, with a P value of zero point one nine. People were not confidently wrong in the sense of rating themselves highly. They were unsure at the start and still unsure at the end, and most of the steps were still missed. The authors’ conclusion is aimed at that handling risk: untrained adults without experience injecting medications could be at high risk of adverse events if they try to self-administer grey-market peptide semaglutide using only internet information. They also say a larger and more diverse group should be studied, and that other products sold as peptides without a prescription should be checked the same way. Twenty adults in one exercise do not describe every buyer.

A 2026 narrative review in Cureus places that scene in a wider pattern. It is not a trial, and it does not enroll patients. It argues that unregulated peptide use is emerging as a digitally mediated public health concern. Peptide-based medicines, the review says, have important therapeutic roles when they are developed, prescribed, manufactured, and monitored through regulated pathways. The use it is worried about is different. Online biohacking and wellness spaces increasingly promote experimental or weakly evidenced peptides for fat loss, recovery, aesthetics, cognition, performance, and longevity.

The review’s account of how the market works is a chain, not a chemical pathway. Digital promotion, grey-market access, self-injection, stacking, informal titration, product-quality uncertainty, regulatory ambiguity, and weak pharmacovigilance interact, and together they normalize poorly traceable products outside clinical supervision. Stacking, in that description, means using more than one of these products together. Informal titration means changing the amount without a clinician. Those words are a description of what the spaces promote. They are not instructions, and this spotlight is not a protocol.

The review’s central concern is not legitimate peptide medicine. It is consumer experimentation with products of uncertain identity, purity, potency, sterility, and safety. A label can name a peptide while the vial’s contents, strength, and cleanliness remain unknown. The review does not itself assay a product, so it does not establish a contamination rate or a potency error rate. What it establishes, at the level of a narrative review, is that those uncertainties sit on the same path as self-injection and thin adverse-event reporting. Harm can fail to show up in a clean record because the record was never built.

Regulatory status, as these two sources state it, is a split. Regulated peptide therapy is the path of development, prescription, manufacture, and monitoring. Non-prescription peptide semaglutide is described as reachable through a legal loophole, which is not the same thing as an approval for buyers to prepare and inject it themselves. The preparation study does not assign that loophole product a labeled indication. The review does not move experimental peptides promoted for fat loss, cognition, or longevity onto an approval list. An unapproved product sold for research use remains unapproved for consumer self-use wherever these sources speak.

What the sources do not establish is the claim a buyer is usually offered. Neither paper shows that grey-market peptides cause fat loss, faster recovery, clearer thinking, or longer life. The twenty-person study measured steps and confidence, not a health outcome. A low score is evidence about handling, not evidence that the peptide works or does not work. The review does not count how often products are mislabeled, contaminated, or harmful, and its call for clinician awareness, adverse-event reporting, product-quality monitoring, digital risk communication, and proportionate oversight is a recommendation, not a result showing that those safeguards are already in place.

The risks the sources do name are plain. In the observed adults, mistakes lined up with a wrong dose, a needle stick, or an infection. Across the market the review describes, identity, purity, potency, and sterility are uncertain, and pharmacovigilance is weak. A research-use label on a page is a commercial category. It is not a human-trial result.

What it is: Research-use and grey-market peptides are products sold outside prescription, manufacture, and monitoring as a medicine.
Humans given it: Twenty adults were scored while preparing non-prescription peptide semaglutide, and the narrative review treated no patients.
Regulatory status: A legal loophole is described as allowing peptide semaglutide to be bought without a prescription, which is not an approval for self-use.
Risks: Missed preparation steps could mean a wrong dose, a needle stick, or an infection, and identity, purity, potency, and sterility are uncertain.
What it does not show: Neither source shows a health benefit, a contamination rate, or that these products are safe to inject at home.

### Worth Knowing
- A cross-sectional congress comparison links GLP-1 use with more reported nail and hair problems, which means an association in people who already have obesity or diabetes, not proof the drugs caused the change.
- An observational surgical-record analysis links GLP-1 use with slightly lower odds of combined heart and infection problems after planned surgery, which is a small absolute difference in matched records, not evidence that the drugs protect someone heading to an operation.
- A small observed test of grey-market peptide semaglutide found untrained adults missing most preparation steps, which is a handling-risk finding about products outside a prescription pathway, not evidence those products treat anything.

### Evidence Ledger
- In a scored observation of twenty adults, people completed fifteen of thirty-four preparation steps for non-prescription peptide semaglutide, with errors that could mean a wrong dose, a needle stick, or an infection; human observation, not a treatment trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42541373
- A narrative review describes unregulated peptide use as digitally promoted consumer experimentation with products of uncertain identity, purity, potency, sterility, and safety, distinct from regulated peptide medicines; narrative review, not a trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42437212

Evidence is a rung, not a slogan: a congress comparison, a surgical record, a mouse result, and a preparation test each answer a different question.

# Peptides Weekly
> **Three to four extra rare vision-loss cases per ten thousand showed up in an observational GLP-1 study.**

**What You Need to Know:** Three to four extra rare vision-loss cases per ten thousand showed up in an observational GLP-1 study. The link was seen in adults with type 2 diabetes and does not prove the drugs injured the optic nerve. Elsewhere this week, an investigational oral GLP-1 program stopped a mid-stage study, and the healing peptide BPC-157 remains a story of laboratory and rodent work rather than a proven human medicine.

### The Week in Peptides
**US study links GLP-1 drugs to rare vision loss: UA.NEWS:** Rutgers researchers, writing in Annals of Internal Medicine and reported by ScienceDaily and UA.NEWS, looked at US adults ages 18 to 65 with type 2 diabetes who had recently started medicines for the disease. In that observational comparison, starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist was associated with a small rise in ischemic optic neuropathy, a rare condition from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve. Chintan Dave of Rutgers said the increase was about three to four additional cases per 10,000 patients over 18 months, and that the condition can involve sudden vision loss. Semaglutide, sold as Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, are approved medicines used to control blood sugar and body weight; the same class can also reduce the risk of certain cardiovascular and kidney problems. More than 80 percent of ischemic optic neuropathy cases, on estimates cited by UA.NEWS, are the nonarteritic anterior form, and recorded cases were more often in men and in people ages 50 to 65. The authors said the association does not prove a direct causal effect, because other health conditions may have shaped the results, and they advised not delaying an eye exam after a sudden change in vision. Source: [ua.news](https://ua.news/en/health/doslidzhennia-v-ssha-poviazalo-glp-1-z-ridkisnoiu-vtratoiu-zoru-sciencedaily) Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261014015521.htm)

**Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades: ScienceDaily:** Researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a peptide called P3 that had been treated as harmless. This is not a human trial: the report describes P3 forming harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and possibly damaging brain cells. Amyloid beta has been the long-standing target of Alzheimer’s drug work that often disappointed, and this write-up puts P3 beside that peptide as another possible contributor. The piece does not present a treatment result in people. Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/10/261013015838.htm)

**Verdiva ends mid-stage study of oral GLP-1 amid ‘market evolution’: BioSpace:** Verdiva has ended a mid-stage study of an oral GLP-1, citing “market evolution.” That is a company decision about an investigational program, not a published randomized result and not an approval. Source: [biospace.com](https://www.biospace.com/drug-development/verdiva-ends-mid-stage-study-of-oral-glp-1-amid-market-evolution)

**As FDA Weighs Wider Peptide Access, Adverse Event Reports and Two Las Vegas Intubations Sharpen Safety Questions: Medical Daily:** Medical Daily reports that the FDA is weighing wider peptide access while adverse-event reports and two Las Vegas intubations sharpen safety questions, in a piece tied to BPC-157. This is news reporting of harm reports and a policy question, not a clinical trial. Unregulated peptide products carry purity and contamination risks that sit beside any access decision. Source: [medicaldaily.com](https://www.medicaldaily.com/fda-peptide-decision-bpc-157-harm-reports-las-vegas-intubations-479941)

**FDA Peptide Compounding Policy: What a Temporary Enforcement Reprieve Could Mean for Pharmacies: Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney PC:** A legal briefing describes a temporary FDA enforcement reprieve in peptide compounding policy and what it could mean for pharmacies. That is a regulatory-policy report, not evidence that a compounded peptide works or is safe. Compounded products are not the same thing as an approved, fully reviewed medicine. Source: [bipc.com](https://www.bipc.com/fda-peptide-compounding-policy-what-a-temporary-enforcement-reprive-could-mean-for-pharmacies)

**MU Health Care physician warns against use of unregulated peptides: KOMU 8:** A physician at MU Health Care has warned against use of unregulated peptides. The warning is clinical commentary reported by a local news outlet, not a new trial. Unregulated products can differ in purity and contamination from anything studied under a regulator’s rules. Source: [komu.com](https://www.komu.com/news/consumer/mu-health-care-physician-warns-against-use-of-unregulated-peptides/article_0274fbda-5d79-512d-94b1-fd3dc2aa4946.html)

### Peptide Spotlight: BPC-157: Popular, Unapproved, Mostly Animal Data
BPC-157 is a pentadecapeptide of 15 amino acids, a partial sequence of a body-protection compound discovered in and isolated from human gastric juice.

In plain terms, the research groups studying it treat it as a healing signal that also touches blood-vessel chemistry. A 1997 rat study in the European Journal of Pharmacology found that, in stomach-tissue homogenates, BPC-157 induced nitric-oxide generation comparable to L-arginine, and that L-NAME, which blocks nitric-oxide synthase, did not inhibit that peptide effect the way it inhibited L-arginine. Combining the peptide with L-arginine blunted nitric-oxide synthesis in that in vitro setup. In the same paper’s rat experiments, the peptide reduced ethanol-induced gastric lesions and altered blood-pressure responses to L-NAME and L-arginine in a pattern that was not identical to L-arginine itself. A 2014 review in Current Pharmaceutical Design frames this as participation in the nitric-oxide system’s response to lost vascular integrity: depending on the injury model, the authors describe less thrombosis or less bleeding and thrombocytopenia. That review also says the peptide stimulates egr-1 and naB2 genes. A 2018 review in Current Pharmaceutical Design adds angiogenic growth-factor signaling—EGF, FGF, and VEGF—as the comparison set, and says BPC-157’s own angiogenic effect shows up in the healing models those authors reviewed.

The strongest evidence in these abstracts is still preclinical, and it is uneven. The 2011 tendon study is ex vivo and in vitro work on rat Achilles-tendon fibroblasts, not a trial in people. BPC-157 accelerated outgrowth from tendon explants. It did not directly change fibroblast proliferation on an MTT assay. Cells treated with it survived hydrogen-peroxide stress better. Migration rose in a dose-dependent way on a transwell assay, spreading on culture dishes accelerated, and F-actin formed. Phosphorylation of FAK and paxillin rose as the amount of peptide rose, while total protein did not change. The authors’ conclusion is that outgrowth, stress survival, and migration are likely mediated by the FAK-paxillin pathway. Separately, a 2026 critical review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, with searches through 24 June 2026, evaluates rodent ischemia-reperfusion and related vascular-injury models. Across that literature, administration was associated with less oxidative injury, shifts in nitric-oxide-related vessel responses, lower inflammatory and apoptotic markers, and changes in VEGF/VEGFR2-Akt-eNOS-related signaling. Organ-specific reports in that review include biochemical and histological protection in lower-extremity skeletal-muscle ischemia-reperfusion, less distant-organ injury after limb ischemia-reperfusion, neuronal and functional effects in hippocampal ischemia-reperfusion, vascular and tissue responses in intestinal and colonic ischemia-reperfusion, and hemodynamic and histological effects in a hepatic Pringle-maneuver model. The reviewers did not pool the studies: organs, doses, routes, timing, and outcomes were too heterogeneous. They also flag short observation, single-dose designs, and incompletely described risk of bias, and they say major-vessel occlusion models are not the same as conventional organ-specific ischemia-reperfusion.

A 2018 review claims BPC-157 was consistently effective, given alone, across acute and chronic injury models of esophagus, stomach, duodenum, and lower gut, by intraperitoneal, oral, or local routes, and that the same regimens improved tendon, ligament, and bone healing in the work reviewed. Those are animal and experimental models summarized by the reviewers, not outcomes measured in patients. A 2013 review in Current Pharmaceutical Design calls BPC-157 an anti-ulcer peptide “proven in clinical trials to be both safe in inflammatory bowel disease” under the codes PL-10, PLD-116, and PL 14736, and in wound healing, and says no toxicity has been reported and an LD1 was not achieved. That is a review’s assertion. The abstract does not report how many people were enrolled, what was measured, or what the trials found beyond that safety claim. The same review argues it could counter several NSAID injuries in stomach, duodenum, intestine, liver, and brain, plus effects on bleeding and thrombosis, again from the experimental work the authors assemble. A 2014 review is explicit that translating nitric-oxide modulation into better clinical performance “remains to be determined.”

A 2026 materials paper in 3 Biotech is not a healing trial. It built a chitosan hydrogel carrying BPC-157, saw a porous structure, and by infrared spectroscopy found hydrogen bonding between the peptide and the chitosan backbone. Water-vapor transmission was 2,270 ± 35 g/m²/day. Encapsulation was 98.9 ± 0.8 percent, with 81.2 ± 2.9 percent released within 24 hours. Antibacterial inhibition reached 45.9 percent against Escherichia coli and 65.0 percent against Staphylococcus aureus. Hemolysis was under 5 percent, which the authors read as acceptable hemocompatibility in that lab test. Those are physicochemical and in vitro antibacterial findings.

These abstracts do not establish BPC-157 as an approved medicine. Medical Daily’s report this week, kept separate above, ties adverse-event reports and two Las Vegas intubations to questions about wider peptide access and BPC-157; that reporting is not efficacy evidence. Authors of the older reviews describe a high preclinical safety margin. That is not the same as a completed human safety record, and it says nothing about purity or contamination when a peptide is sold outside a controlled study.

What it is: BPC-157 is a 15-amino-acid fragment related to a peptide found in human gastric juice.
Humans given it: Named inflammatory-bowel-disease trial codes appear in a 2013 review, which does not report how many people were studied.
Risks: Preclinical “no toxicity” claims are not a human safety proof, and harm reports are already part of the access debate.
What it does not show: Rodent and cell findings do not show that BPC-157 heals tendon, gut, or ischemia-reperfusion injury in people.

### Worth Knowing
- An observational association between starting a GLP-1 medicine and a rare optic-nerve injury, in adults with type 2 diabetes, is a signal to understand, not proof the drug caused the injury.
- A rare association can still matter when a medicine is used widely, which is why the study authors called the finding clinically important even while describing the absolute risk as low.
- Stopping a mid-stage oral GLP-1 study is a development decision about an investigational peptide drug, not evidence that the class failed or succeeded in people.

### Evidence Ledger
- BPC-157, a 15-amino-acid gastric-juice peptide, sped tendon-fibroblast outgrowth, stress survival, and migration in rat cell and explant work via FAK-paxillin phosphorylation, without changing proliferation on an MTT assay; ex vivo/in vitro animal-cell evidence. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/21030672
- In rats and in gastric-mucosa homogenates, BPC-157 interfered with nitric-oxide effects on gastric lesions and blood pressure in a pattern distinct from L-arginine, and L-NAME did not block its nitric-oxide generation the way it blocked L-arginine; animal and in vitro evidence. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/9298922
- A review links BPC-157 to nitric-oxide homeostasis after vascular injury and states that clinical translation remains to be determined; narrative review of preclinical work. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/23755725
- A review says only BPC-157, among the peptides compared, was consistently effective in the gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal injury models surveyed; narrative review of experimental models. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/29998800
- A review asserts clinical-trial safety in inflammatory bowel disease under codes PL-10, PLD-116, and PL 14736, and assembles experimental counter-effects to NSAID injury, while reporting no achieved LD1; review assertion, trial headcount not in the abstract. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/22950504
- A 2026 critical review finds rodent ischemia-reperfusion studies associated BPC-157 with less oxidative, inflammatory, and apoptotic injury and with VEGF-related signaling changes, but judges the evidence heterogeneous and bias-prone; preclinical review, no meta-analysis. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42794771
- A chitosan/BPC-157 hydrogel showed high encapsulation, substantial 24-hour release, antibacterial inhibition, and hemolysis under 5 percent in laboratory tests; materials and in vitro evidence, not a human trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42555375

Knowing which rung a peptide claim sits on is the useful habit this week.

# Peptides Weekly
> **Unapproved peptides could reach temporary sale while treatment claims are still not fully safety tested.**

**What You Need to Know:** Unapproved peptides could reach temporary sale while treatment claims are still not fully safety tested. Political Wire, quoting The Washington Post, describes a drafting process for previously restricted peptides, not a completed approval and not a patient trial. Separate reporting the same week covers an FDA advisory panel, a cancer-risk association, dissolving oral films, and diet after GLP-1 treatment.

### The Week in Peptides
**Trump administration paving way for temporary sale of some unapproved peptides:** The Washington Post
This is a policy report, not a human trial. The Washington Post headline calls the products unapproved peptides, and Political Wire quotes that paper as saying the Trump administration is crafting plans for temporary sale of certain previously restricted peptides while federal health officials hammer out new regulations. The quoted report says such a move would allow some compounding pharmacies to dispense certain peptides marketed as new medical treatments and wellness products. It also says the claims for what they treat have not been fully safety tested. On October 1 this show was following compounding rules; today's addition is that temporary-sale drafting, with the products still described as unapproved and incompletely safety tested. Source: [washingtonpost.com](https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/10/07/trump-administration-paving-way-temporary-sale-some-unapproved-peptides/) https://politicalwire.com/2026/10/07/trump-moves-to-allow-sale-of-untested-peptides/

**HIMS Stock Climbs Overnight As FDA Advisory Panel Backs 4 Peptides:** Stocktwits
Stocktwits reported a regulatory-panel action, not a published patient trial: an FDA advisory panel backed four peptides. The same item tied that backing to an overnight climb in Hims shares and a short position by Martin Shkreli. Medical Economics, the same day, reported that the FDA would convene an expert panel on wider access to peptides. Those are reports of panel process and market reaction, not measured clinical outcomes. Source: [stocktwits.com](https://stocktwits.com/news-articles/markets/equity/hims-fda-panel-4-peptides-martin-shkreli-short/cZZYKkgR7Uy) https://www.medicaleconomics.com/view/team-based-care-model-cuts-blood-pressure-in-high-risk-populations-fda-to-convene-expert-panel-on-wider-access-to-peptides-florida-nursing-assistant-sentenced-in-11-4m-medicare-brace-fraud-scheme-morning-medical-update

**GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use Linked to Lower Colorectal Cancer Risk in Patients With Inflammatory Bowel Disease:** The ASCO Post
The ASCO Post reported a link between GLP-1 receptor agonist use and lower colorectal cancer risk in patients with inflammatory bowel disease. A reported link is an association-level claim, not a randomized trial result with an effect size in this item, and it does not show that the drugs caused fewer cancers. Source: [ascopost.com](https://ascopost.com/news/october-2026/glp-1-receptor-agonist-use-linked-to-lower-colorectal-cancer-risk-in-patients-with-inflammatory-bowel-disease/)

**Oral peptide strips promise needle-free delivery, but what do the FDA and researchers say?:** Sacramento Bee
The Sacramento Bee and the Raleigh News & Observer published consumer explainers, not trial reports, on oral peptide strips. The Bee's headline says the strips promise needle-free delivery and frames what the FDA and researchers say as the question under discussion. The News & Observer headline describes dissolving films and asks how peptide strips work. Neither item, in the text available here, is a measured human efficacy result. Source: [amp.sacbee.com](https://amp.sacbee.com/entertainment/article317516843.html) https://amp.newsobserver.com/living/article317516887.html

**Post-GLP-1 weight regain could be mitigated by diet:** FoodNavigator.com
FoodNavigator reported that weight regain after GLP-1 treatment could be mitigated by diet. That headline is a possibility claim in a news item, not a randomized human trial result with a measured effect presented here. Source: [foodnavigator.com](https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2026/10/07/post-glp-1-weight-regain-mitigated-by-diet/)

### Peptide Spotlight: Collagen Peptides as Supplements
Collagen peptides in these papers are short collagen fragments taken by mouth and studied as supplements, including as a nutricosmetic ingredient, not as a named approved drug.

The 2015 Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology paper says preclinical work had already suggested these peptides can improve skin barrier function, induce synthesis of collagen and hyaluronic acid, and promote fibroblast growth and migration. In human skin explants, an ex vivo model, collagen peptides induced collagen and glycosaminoglycan production. That is a tissue-level mechanism, not a proof of what happens after digestion in a living person. The clinical papers then look at downstream markers: skin hydration and dermal collagen structure, hair gloss and elasticity, and blood markers of bone turnover and inflammation.

Strongest human evidence in this set is randomized and placebo-controlled. In two placebo-controlled clinical trials reported in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology in 2015, oral collagen peptide supplementation increased skin hydration after 8 weeks, measured by corneometry. Collagen density in the dermis rose, and fragmentation of the dermal collagen network fell, after 4 weeks, measured by high-resolution ultrasound and reflectance confocal microscopy. Both of those structural changes persisted after 12 weeks.

In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in the International Journal of Stem Cells, Korean adults aged 19 to 60 with mild to moderate hair damage and without alopecia received low-molecular-weight collagen peptide GT for 24 weeks. Compared with placebo, the treatment group had significant improvements in hair gloss, measured with a gloss meter and scanning electron microscopy, and in hair elasticity, assessed by tensile strength and hair diameter. Subjective scores also moved toward better gloss, elasticity, thickness, texture, fullness, and appearance, and scalp elasticity rose in the treatment group. No treatment-related adverse events were observed. The authors call that course safe and effective for overall hair condition in people with damaged hair and without alopecia. The same abstract says earlier preclinical work found that low-molecular-weight fish collagen peptides promoted hair regrowth in animals or laboratory models by activating proliferative signaling and suppressing inhibitory pathways, and that clinical efficacy for hair damage had not been clearly established before this trial. This human trial measured damage, gloss, and elasticity, not regrowth in alopecia.

In a pilot randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Frontiers in Nutrition, 22 endurance-trained premenopausal women aged 18 to 35 who ran at least 35 miles a week were assigned to collagen peptides or an isocaloric maltodextrin placebo for four weeks. Blood was drawn in the early follicular phase. A group-by-time interaction for P1NP, a marker of bone formation, was significant at p = 0.04, with an increase in the collagen group and no change on placebo. CTX-1, a marker of bone breakdown, showed no significant interaction (p = 0.13). The results text reports a significant interaction for IL-6 (p = 0.03). It also reports a significant interaction for sRANKL (p = 0.046) and, later, no significant interaction for sRANKL, osteoprotegerin, or the sRANKL/osteoprotegerin ratio, so the osteoclast-signal finding is not cleanly established in this write-up. The discussion says short-term supplementation increased a bone-formation marker, altered osteoclast-related signaling, and reduced IL-6, and that structural bone outcomes still need larger trials.

In a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in the British Journal of Nutrition, 53 men with sarcopenia, mean age 72.2 years (standard deviation 4.68), completed 12 weeks of guided resistance training three sessions a week plus either collagen peptides or a silica placebo. Everyone who finished improved: fat-free mass, bone mass, isokinetic quadriceps strength, and sensory motor control rose, and fat mass fell (all P < 0.01). The collagen arm changed more than placebo: fat-free mass +4.2 kg (standard deviation 2.31) versus +2.9 kg (standard deviation 1.84); quadriceps strength +16.5 newton-metres (standard deviation 12.9) versus +7.3 (standard deviation 13.2); fat mass −5.4 kg (standard deviation 3.17) versus −3.5 kg (standard deviation 2.16); each comparison P < 0.05. That extra change is a training-plus-supplement result in older men, not an effect of collagen peptides alone.

What is not established: these abstracts do not show fracture prevention, treatment of alopecia, or a drug-style disease indication. Skin and hair findings are appearance and tissue measures. The bone pilot is 22 women over four weeks and does not include structural bone outcomes. The sarcopenia result cannot be separated from the resistance program. One abstract contradicts itself on sRANKL.

These papers present collagen peptides as oral supplements and a nutricosmetic ingredient. They do not describe an approved drug use. The hair trial recorded no treatment-related adverse events. The other abstracts emphasize benefits and do not catalogue harms. Unregulated supplement products can differ from the material used in a trial; these papers do not test marketplace purity.

What it is: Collagen peptides here are oral collagen fragments studied as supplements, including a nutricosmetic ingredient, not as a named approved drug.
Humans given it: Human data in these sources include 22 women in a four-week bone-marker pilot and 53 older men in a 12-week training trial, plus placebo-controlled trials in adults with skin aging and in adults with damaged hair without alopecia.
What it does not show: They do not show fracture prevention, regrowth in alopecia, a peptide-only muscle effect, or that a biomarker change is a clinical outcome.

### Worth Knowing
A reported link between GLP-1 receptor agonist use and lower colorectal cancer risk in inflammatory bowel disease is an association, so it does not establish that the drugs prevent cancer.
Human collagen-peptide trials in this set measured skin hydration and dermal structure, hair gloss and elasticity, bone-turnover markers, and training-related body composition, which is a different evidence rung from a product claim about disease treatment.
Policy reporting on temporary sale and advisory-panel backing describes access and process, not a human efficacy result for those peptides.

### Evidence Ledger
- In two placebo-controlled trials, oral collagen peptides increased skin hydration after 8 weeks and improved dermal collagen density and fragmentation from 4 weeks through 12 weeks; ex vivo human skin explants showed induced collagen and glycosaminoglycan production. Evidence level: randomized human trials plus ex vivo tissue. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26362110
- In a randomized placebo-controlled trial of Korean adults with damaged hair and without alopecia, 24 weeks of low-molecular-weight collagen peptide GT improved gloss, elasticity, and scalp elasticity versus placebo, with no treatment-related adverse events. Evidence level: randomized human trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42624827
- In a four-week pilot randomized trial of 22 premenopausal endurance runners, collagen peptides raised P1NP versus placebo (p = 0.04) and showed an IL-6 interaction (p = 0.03), without a CTX-1 interaction, and without structural bone outcomes. Evidence level: pilot randomized human trial. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42221768
- In 53 older men with sarcopenia, 12 weeks of resistance training plus collagen peptides increased fat-free mass and quadriceps strength and reduced fat mass more than training plus placebo. Evidence level: randomized human trial, combination with training. https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26353786

A peptide claim is only as strong as the rung it was measured on.

# Peptides Weekly
> **Nail detachment was over four times more common in people using GLP-1 drugs.**

**What You Need to Know:** A controlled study found nail detachment more than four times as often among people using GLP-1 drugs. The same week brought a muscle-loss trial beside semaglutide, a randomized look at how semaglutide meets the kidney, and two reminders that a population trend and a protein-design paper are not treatment results. None of this is a reason to start, stop, or change a medicine.

### The Week in Peptides
**Nail detachment over four times more common among GLP-1 users, first controlled study finds: Medical Xpress**
Medical Xpress reported on September 30, 2026, that nail detachment was over four times more common among GLP-1 users. The report calls this the first controlled study of that comparison, so the evidence level is a controlled human study, not a cell experiment and not an animal result. A controlled comparison can show a difference between groups; it does not, by itself, prove why a nail lifted in any one person. GLP-1 drugs are peptide medicines people already meet in clinics and online, which is why a new harm signal belongs next to the weight and glucose claims. Source: [medicalxpress.com](https://medicalxpress.com/news/2026-09-detachment-common-glp-users.html)

**Regeneron drug halves muscle loss in combination with Novo's semaglutide in trial: Reuters**
In a new trial result, rather than another pass at weight-loss totals, Regeneron's drug halved muscle loss in combination with Novo's semaglutide, Reuters reported on September 30, 2026. That is a human trial finding. Medical Xpress names the Regeneron drug trevogrumab and describes it as anti-myostatin, a blocker of myostatin, and says it can help preserve lean mass during and after semaglutide-induced weight loss. Source: [reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/regeneron-drug-halves-muscle-loss-combination-with-novos-semaglutide-trial-2026-09-30/)

**Effects of semaglutide on kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: a randomized placebo-controlled trial: Nature Medicine**
After earlier work on blood-vessel markers, Nature Medicine published online on October 1, 2026, a randomized trial in people with type 2 diabetes that probed the kidney-protective mechanisms of semaglutide. The methods named in the journal's notice are histology, multiparametric MRI, and transcriptomics, so this is a randomized human study of mechanism, not a headline that counts how many people reached kidney failure. A mechanism finding can explain a path. It is not, on this notice alone, an outcome result. Source: [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-026-04674-2)

**Mauritius first country with decreasing diabetes prevalence per WHO criteria: The Lancet**
The Lancet reported a finding presented at EASD 2026: Mauritius is the first country to show a decreasing prevalence of diabetes and intermediate hyperglycaemia over time. The comparison used OGTT-based diagnostic criteria recommended by WHO, which the post calls the objective gold standard, and points to more in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. This is an observational population result, not a peptide trial and not evidence that any drug caused the decline. Source: [t.co](https://t.co/YrWo7z2VzG)

**Watermarking AI-generated proteins to establish provenance: Nature**
Eric Topol pointed to a Nature paper, by Pushmeet and colleagues at Google DeepMind, on watermarking AI-generated proteins while preserving their function, so later readers can establish provenance. A companion Nature news piece sits beside the research article. This is a methods paper about designed proteins, not a human trial of a medicine, and it does not show that a watermarked protein is safe or effective in people. Source: [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10965-y)

### Peptide Spotlight: How to Read Peptide Evidence
Sleep disorders affect more than 70 million people globally, a 2026 review in Brain reports, and that review is a clean place to start when a peptide claim arrives with the word "study" and nothing else. The review's point is not a sleep drug. It is a ladder. Optogenetics and chemogenetics have given precise control of sleep-wake transitions in animal models, which shows that sleep can be modulated in those models by targeted circuit manipulation. The same review says translation of those findings to human applications faces substantial challenges. Some principles appear conserved across species. Significant differences in circuit architecture, technical capabilities, and regulatory constraints still call for different human approaches. A beautiful animal switch is not a human result.

Read the rung before the adjective. A cell or in vitro finding asks whether a pathway can fire in a dish or a tissue prep. An animal finding asks whether that pathway matters in a living non-human body under controlled conditions. A small human study asks whether a signal appears in people, often on a biomarker, a scan, or a short safety check. An outcome trial asks whether people have fewer of the events that change a life: organ failure, hospitalization, death, or a predefined clinical score. Association is not cause. A biomarker change is not an outcome. Those distinctions are the whole method.

The stroke literature shows why the middle rungs are not worthless and also not final. A review in Cellular and Molecular Neurobiology says the contributory role of inflammatory and immune processes in ischemic stroke was demonstrated in vitro and in animal models, and was confirmed in humans. That is one of the stronger patterns a methods review can offer: the same broad process shows up at more than one rung. Even then, the authors say translation of experimental findings to the human disease is still a difficult step, and further investigations are required to fill the gaps. Confirmation of a process is not a recipe for a treatment, and it is not permission to treat a damage-associated molecular pattern paper as a clinic protocol.

Animal prediction fails often enough that the failure has its own review. In Biochemical Pharmacology, McGonigle and colleagues describe animal models as historically central to pathophysiology, target identification, and in vivo evaluation of new chemical entities, then note the criticism that followed clinical trial failures of compounds with promising preclinical profiles. The limited ability, they write, is about predicting efficacy, safety, and toxicity in humans. Their practical advice stays on the evidence ladder: test hypotheses in more than one disease model, evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic relationships, and develop validated disease-associated biomarkers earlier so target engagement is measured rather than assumed. The predictive value of an animal model is only as useful as the context in which it is interpreted. That sentence is the one to keep when a peptide advertisement says "shown in animals."

Biomarkers need the same humility. A 2026 review in Lab Animal, on tuberculosis markers across species, defines a biomarker as a measurable indicator of a biological state or condition, useful for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment monitoring. It also says clinical studies are constrained by cost, ethics, and sampling, which is why animal models exist, and that species-specific differences are real advantages and real limits. The conclusion is integration: animal data and human data have to be read together. A marker that moves in a model is a candidate. It is not yet a diagnosis in a person.

Mechanism studies can be precise and still sit below outcomes. A Pharmacotherapy review of vancomycin-induced kidney injury describes preclinical toxicodynamic work in which injury tracks with drug accumulation in proximal tubule cells, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, and with higher maximal concentrations and areas under the curve more than with troughs. That is mechanism, mostly from preclinical models. The same review says there is a poor understanding of the mechanistic drivers in ordinary clinical use and several gaps before the drug could be made less toxic. A pathway mapped in an animal kidney does not tell a listener the rate of injury in people, and it does not authorize a dosing change. This spotlight is about how to read that gap, not about vancomycin care.

What is not established is any universal conversion rate from one rung to the next. The sleep review does not claim that conserved circuits guarantee a human benefit. The stroke review does not claim that human confirmation of inflammation has closed the translational gap. The animal-model review does not claim that better biomarkers will rescue every failed prediction. None of these papers is a peptide outcome trial, and none of them ranks a named peptide medicine.

This is not a compound, so it has no approval, no label, and no regulator's indication. The risk is misreading. Treating a cell result as an animal result, an animal result as a human result, or a biomarker shift as a clinical outcome is how a listener gets ahead of the evidence. Unregulated products add a separate problem the method cannot fix: a study of a pure research peptide does not describe the vial in a grey-market ad. The useful habit is to ask four questions of every claim: what was studied, in what kind of system, what was measured, and whether that measurement was the outcome a person would care about.

What it is: It is a way of ranking a peptide claim by the kind of study behind it, from cells and animals up to human outcomes.
Humans given it: No people were assigned this method as a treatment, because it is a reading habit rather than a compound in a trial.
Regulatory status: It is not a medicine, and the sources describe no approval, label, or authorized use for it.
Risks: The practical risk is mistaking a lower rung, or a biomarker shift, for proof that people benefit or are unharmed.
What it does not show: It does not show that a conserved animal mechanism, or a human confirmation of a pathway, is itself a clinical outcome.

### Worth Knowing
- A controlled human comparison can put a nail finding on the map for GLP-1 users without proving the cause in any single person.
- A human trial that tracks lean mass is measuring something a scale does not, so weight change and muscle change are different facts.
- A randomized mechanism study in people with type 2 diabetes can show how semaglutide meets kidney tissue and still not be a count of kidney-failure outcomes.
- A country-level drop in diabetes prevalence, read with glucose-tolerance testing, is population surveillance, not evidence for or against a peptide.

### Evidence Ledger
- Sleep disorders affect more than 70 million people, and animal circuit tools face substantial barriers to human translation, at the level of a review of animal and human stimulation studies: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41738647
- Inflammatory mechanisms in ischemic stroke were shown in vitro and in animals and confirmed in humans, while translation remains difficult, at review level: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32996044
- Animal models have a limited ability to predict human efficacy, safety, and toxicity after preclinical promise, at review level: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/23954708
- Tuberculosis biomarker work in animals must be integrated with human studies because species differ, at review level: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42243511
- Vancomycin kidney injury is mapped in preclinical models to tubule accumulation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, with clinical gaps remaining, at review level: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32239518

The rung of the study is the result you can use; the molecule's name is not.

# Peptides Weekly
> **Nearly one in six children taking GLP-1 drugs show nutritional deficiencies in a new study.**

**What You Need to Know:** A retrospective analysis found nutritional deficiencies in almost 17 percent of children prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight loss or diabetes. The finding comes from claims data and highlights a measurable gap in monitoring for younger patients. Separate reports note rising adverse-event filings for semaglutide in Sweden and online platforms offering the medicines without physician review.

### The Week in Peptides
**GLP-1 weight loss and diabetes drugs linked to nutritional deficiencies in nearly 1 in 6 children: ScienceDaily**
An observational analysis of insurance claims data linked GLP-1 receptor agonists to documented nutritional deficiencies in nearly one in six children. The study examined real-world prescribing records rather than a controlled trial. Researchers tracked filled prescriptions and subsequent laboratory results for vitamin and mineral shortfalls. No causal mechanism was established in the dataset. The analysis covered multiple GLP-1 agents used for type 2 diabetes or weight management. Claims databases capture routine care but miss unrecorded supplements or dietary changes. Source: [sciencedaily.com](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/09/260923035926.htm)

**Websites ease GLP-1 access without doctor oversight, Yale study finds: Yale Daily News**
A Yale review of online platforms found multiple sites supplying GLP-1 medicines after only a questionnaire and without an in-person or video visit by a licensed clinician. The study documented the absence of required medical evaluation in the sales process. Researchers classified the model as direct-to-consumer access that bypasses standard oversight. Platforms required self-reported height, weight and medical history but did not verify details with a prescriber. The review covered several high-traffic sites operating in the United States. No regulatory action was described in the report. Source: [yaledailynews.com](https://yaledailynews.com/articles/websites-help-glp-1-access-without-doctor-oversight-yale-study-finds)

**Sweden sees rise in reported adverse reactions to semaglutide: euractiv.com**
Swedish pharmacovigilance records show an increase in adverse-reaction reports tied to semaglutide in the most recent reporting period. The data come from the national spontaneous reporting system and do not include confirmed causality assessments. Reports included gastrointestinal events and other side effects already known from clinical trials. The national agency collects voluntary submissions from healthcare professionals and patients. Source: [euractiv.com](https://www.euractiv.com/news/sweden-sees-rise-in-reported-adverse-reactions-to-semaglutide/)

**Peptides Promise Superhero Healing Powers. The Dangerous Reality Does Not Match the Hype.: Outside Magazine**
An investigative feature examined unregulated peptide products sold for recovery and performance. The reporting contrasted marketing claims with documented cases of contamination and adverse effects in users. No controlled human trials supported the promoted benefits for the products discussed. The article described products labeled for research use only that reached consumers through online vendors. Laboratory testing cited in the piece revealed inconsistent purity across batches. Cyclists and other athletes were among the users interviewed for the story. Source: [velo.outsideonline.com](https://velo.outsideonline.com/road/road-training/peptide-guide-for-cyclists/)

**IGF2BP3 drives macrophage M1 polarization to promote intracranial aneurysm rupture through m6A-mediated NPY1R stabilization: Peptides**
A laboratory study in cell and animal models identified IGF2BP3 as a regulator that stabilizes NPY1R mRNA and shifts macrophages toward an M1 phenotype linked to aneurysm rupture. The work used molecular assays and rodent aneurysm models. Human data were not reported. Researchers measured changes in m6A modification on the NPY1R transcript after IGF2BP3 knockdown. Macrophage polarization was assessed by surface markers and cytokine profiles. The pathway was tested in both in-vitro cultures and in-vivo aneurysm induction. Source: [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0196978126000598?dgcid=rss_sd_all)

### Peptide Spotlight: Semaglutide and the GLP-1 Class
Semaglutide is a long-acting analogue of the gut hormone GLP-1. It binds the GLP-1 receptor on pancreatic beta cells to increase glucose-dependent insulin release and on alpha cells to suppress glucagon. The same receptor activation in the brain reduces appetite and slows gastric emptying.

In the SUSTAIN-6 trial, 3,297 adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk received once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide or placebo for 104 weeks. The primary composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke occurred in 6.6 percent of the semaglutide group versus 8.9 percent of placebo, confirming noninferiority and suggesting superiority. In the SELECT trial, 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity but without diabetes received 2.4 mg weekly semaglutide or placebo for a mean 39.8 months. The same composite endpoint occurred in 6.5 percent versus 8.0 percent, establishing a cardiovascular benefit in this population.

The PIONEER program tested oral semaglutide in more than 8,000 adults across eight phase 3 trials lasting up to 78 weeks. Doses of 7 mg and 14 mg once daily lowered HbA1c and body weight more than placebo, sitagliptin, empagliflozin, liraglutide and dulaglutide. Gastrointestinal events were the most frequent side effects and were usually transient.

A post-hoc analysis of a 32-week randomized trial found that semaglutide increased the reactive hyperemic index from baseline but the change did not reach significance versus placebo; E-selectin fell significantly versus placebo while other cell-adhesion markers showed mixed responses.

Cost-effectiveness modeling using SURMOUNT-5 head-to-head data estimated that maximum-tolerated tirzepatide produced lower total costs and higher quality-adjusted life years than maximum-tolerated semaglutide in adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes.

What it is: Semaglutide is a synthetic GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide used to improve glycemic control and reduce cardiovascular risk.
Humans given it: More than 25,000 adults participated in the phase 3 trials summarized in the abstracts.
Regulatory status: Approved in multiple countries for type 2 diabetes and for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition.
Risks: Transient gastrointestinal effects are the most common; cardiovascular safety has been established in large outcome trials.
What it does not show: The abstracts do not establish long-term effects on nutritional status in children or comparative safety versus newer multi-agonists outside the modeled populations.

### Worth Knowing
- An observational analysis of insurance claims shows nutritional deficiencies appear in nearly one in six children prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists, indicating a need for laboratory monitoring in this age group.
- Spontaneous reporting data from Sweden record a recent increase in adverse-event filings for semaglutide, underscoring the value of ongoing pharmacovigilance for approved GLP-1 medicines.
- Laboratory work on IGF2BP3 and aneurysm rupture illustrates how basic peptide signaling research can identify new molecular targets, though the findings remain at the cell and animal stage.

### Evidence Ledger
- Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27633186)
- In the SELECT trial the same composite occurred in 569 of 8803 semaglutide patients versus 701 of 8801 placebo patients (hazard ratio 0.80). Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37952131)
- Oral semaglutide 7 mg and 14 mg reduced HbA1c and body weight versus multiple active comparators in the PIONEER program. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32267058)

Semaglutide improves cardiovascular outcomes in large randomized trials while its gastrointestinal side effects remain the main tolerability concern.
